`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` skipped a key identifier only once a signature under it had succeeded, so a document repeating one identical failing signature record re-derived that key's material identity and re-ran the verify for every repetition: measured over a 414 KB body, 1000 repetitions of a single all-zero signature cost 2000 key imports, 1000 signature checks and 1617 milliseconds, all on metadata nothing has authenticated yet and all answering `verified: false`. A key is imported once per identifier and a verify is asked once per identifier-and-signature pair, so the same document answers in 5 milliseconds, and a good signature arriving after a bad one under the same key still counts. The pair is named by the decoded signature rather than by its text, because hexadecimal is read in either case and one 64-byte value therefore has up to 2^128 spellings: named by the text, 1000 spellings of one value bought 1000 signature checks over the same body. 1000 genuinely different values are still 1000 checks.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` takes the KEYID to key map the same way it takes the document and the role: held to being a plain object carrying plain values at every identifier the role names, refused as `tuf/bad-input` otherwise. The map's members are read inside a loop that awaits a verification per signature, so a `Proxy` or an accessor there answered each read separately, and the identifier filed under a key is checked against the copy the first read produced. A conforming caller passes plain values and notices nothing.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` resolved a role's identifiers to keys one occurrence at a time, and each resolution deep-copied the key and hashed its canonical form, so an identifier the role repeated asked for that work again although the answer was already filed. Measured, 7500 repetitions of one identifier beside a 500 KB key spent 10.2 seconds inside that resolution, synchronously, before the first await and before anything had authenticated a byte of the document, all inside the one-megabyte metadata size cap. The repeat is a lookup now, and the same document resolves in 6 milliseconds.

A TUF key was imported twice per identifier, once to derive the identity a threshold counts it under and once to check a signature with it, so the asymmetric work a document could ask for before anything authenticated it was twice what it needed to be. Both come from one import now, in the role walk `pki.tuf.updateRoot` makes at adoption as well as in `pki.tuf.verifySignatures`, which also means the key counted and the key verified with cannot be two different keys.

`pki.jose.parseJson` returned an object the toolkit's own option validation refused. The result carries a hidden `then` holding no value, which stops an `await` of it from reaching a replacement installed on `Object.prototype`, and the option check counted that name: a configuration document parsed with this verb and passed to `pki.jose.verify` failed with `jose/bad-input` naming `then` as an unknown option, while the identical document through `JSON.parse` was accepted. A hidden name holding no value is passed over now, at every door that enumerates names rather than only the one this was found through: the option check, the name list a verb builds its accepted forms from, and the copy a verb makes of a caller's options, that copy having no inherited `then` to stand in front of. A `then` that carries a value is still reported as an unknown option, in either visibility, and a parsed document carrying one still keeps it. So is an accessor named `then`, including one whose getter and setter are both absent, which answers each read separately and is the shape the mask exists to replace rather than to resemble. So is a name a verb's list of accepted options carries, since the mask is about a name nothing asked for, and so is one reported by a `Proxy`, whose descriptors say whatever its traps return rather than what it holds.

`pki keygen` records what it wrote at each destination so a failed run removes only the files it created. That record carried no identity until the content was in, and a record with no identity was deleted with no comparison at all, so a run whose write failed removed whatever occupied the path, including a file that had replaced its own. The identity now comes from the creating descriptor, before any content, and the size and timestamp are still recorded once a write returns. A file that replaced the one this run created, changed since, or carries a second name for its content is left where it is and named on stderr, as is one the platform cannot identify after a failed write, and one the cleanup could not examine at all: a path that cannot be read is not a path whose file is gone, and that outcome used to be passed over in silence. The link test asks what is on disk rather than comparing against a count the run recorded, since a name added before the record was taken and removed afterwards made the count fall. An empty path is reported too, a file this run created and something else moved away leaving the same bare path while its content sits somewhere the operator has not been told about. `--out` and `--pub` naming the same file is refused before a key is generated, and a report naming a path keeps to one line, a newline in the name having ended the line early and put what followed where the tool's own output is read.

The same record now covers every file the CLI writes, not only the keys. `pki csr`, `pki issue`, `pki fetch` and `pki sign` with `--out` wrote through a plain overwrite, so a write that failed part way through left a file the run had just created with nothing tracking it: measured, a failing write to a new path left the partial file in place. A path that does not exist is created exclusively and written through its own descriptor, as a key is, and a failed write removes it. A path that DOES exist is still overwritten, which is what those verbs have always done and what separates them from the key verbs, and a file the run did not create is never one it removes. That overwrite goes through a descriptor opened without permission to create, so a path that stops existing between the two calls is retried as the exclusive create it has become rather than written by name into a file nothing is tracking, and a write that fails part way through an existing file now says that the file was overwritten and what is there is incomplete. The bytes go out through the call that writes all of them rather than one that can report a short count and return, which a caller ignoring the count would close as a complete file. A destination that is not a regular file is still written: `/dev/null`, `/dev/stdout` and a FIFO hold no previous content to clear, and truncating one is an error rather than a no-op, so the truncation happens only where there is something to truncate and a destination that refuses a read-write open is written by name as these verbs always did.

`pki issue --csr` now answers what the request asks for instead of dropping it. A request carries the extensions it wants through the RFC 2985 section 5.4.2 extensionRequest attribute, and this path read only the request's subject and public key, building the certificate's extensions from `--san` alone. So `pki csr --key k --subject CN=host.example --san host.example` followed by `pki issue --csr req.der` reported success and issued a certificate with no subjectAltName, which matches no host name: the failure arrived at whatever later presented the certificate rather than at the command that made it. Which requested extensions to honor is the CA's decision, so neither answer is taken by default. `--copy-requested-san` writes the requested subjectAltName into the certificate, converting each name through the same builder that validates a name given on the command line. `--ignore-requested-extensions` issues without what the request asked for. A request that asks for anything neither flag accounts for is refused, naming what was asked and both flags, so a certificate is never issued carrying less than the request asked for while reporting success. A requested name of a form the copy does not write, a directoryName or an otherName, is named and refuses the issuance rather than being left out of the copy. `--san` and `--copy-requested-san` together are refused, both naming the subjectAltName, and both flags require `--csr`, there being no request to answer without one.

`pki <verb> --help` now exits 0 with the usage line on stdout. Every verb reached its usage text through the check for a missing argument, which writes to stderr and exits 1, so a script asking `pki csr --help` could not tell the help it asked for from a csr that failed to run, while top-level `pki --help` answered the same question and exited 0. Help is now answered before the verb runs, for `--help` and `-h` on all eleven verbs that have a usage line, including a verb whose arguments are otherwise complete and a help flag standing where a flag's value belongs. A genuinely missing argument still writes its usage to stderr and exits non-zero.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` now reads the keys the role names rather than the signatures the document lists, so a document's signature list decides which signature each key offers and no longer how many checks run. Reading the document's list let it choose: a signature repeated, or spelled differently, shared a memo, but distinct signatures for one authorized key shared nothing, and each one hashed the whole signed body. Measured, a 1,013,726-byte document carrying a 500 KB body and 2,400 signatures made with a key nobody authorized bought 2,400 key imports and 2,400 signature checks and about a second of synchronous work, inside the one-megabyte size cap and before anything had authenticated a byte of it; 1,000 distinct signatures under one key now cost one check, and 40 keys a role names cost 40. The work follows the document's own size rather than the product of its body and its signature list. The role is the caller's argument, and a root rotation also verifies a candidate against the root role it states itself, which is the check a new root must pass, so that one call's count is the candidate's to state. The verdict is unchanged for a conforming document, which carries one signature per key. The two authorities differ on a key identifier listed more than once and this satisfies both: the specification caps the count at one verified signature from a key identifier and leaves the document readable, the reference implementation refuses it outright, and the first signature an identifier carries is now the one asked. A document that lists a wrong signature for a key ahead of a right one therefore reads as that key not having signed, and a second entry for a key cannot change a count the specification already caps at one.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` reads the artifact once per digest algorithm when checking a message signature. The comparison against the digest a transparency-log entry records runs per attempt, and an attempt that failed it sent the next one over the same bytes again, so the caller's whole file was read once per entry the bundle listed. The entry count is capped at 32, which bounded the factor rather than removing it: a 100 MB artifact was hashed 32 times. The same bytes under the same algorithm are the same digest, so each algorithm an entry names now costs one pass. The comparison against the `messageDigest` the bundle itself carries reads through the same answer: it names its own algorithm, so a bundle whose first entry records the wrong artifact under SHA-512, whose selected entry records the right one under SHA-256, and whose `messageDigest` claims SHA-512 read the artifact three times for two algorithms.

Every byte input to a `pki.ct` verb is bounded before it is copied, not only the ones a caller passed a limit for. The one door they all enter through took its limit as an optional argument, so the inputs that passed none were copied at whatever size arrived: a 32 MiB value supplied as a 32-byte tree head hash allocated 32 MiB, and one supplied as its signature allocated 64 MiB across the two reads, with the same on the chain, pinned-key, leaf-hash and issuer-hash inputs of `verifySth`, `verifySct`, `addChain`, `getSth`, `getProofByHash` and `fetchLogList`. The door now applies the toolkit's DER ceiling when no narrower width is stated, so a verb added later is bounded without being bounded by hand, and a site that knows its own width still states it. An oversized value is refused with `ct/too-large` and nothing is copied.

`pki.hpke.setupS` copies the recipient's key before it reads the options bag, so an option getter cannot change who a message is encrypted to. Reading that bag runs caller code, and a getter on `opts.info` that wrote another recipient's key over the buffer had the setup encapsulate to that other recipient while the caller had named the first: measured, a sender naming one recipient produced a message only the other could open, with every width check passing because both keys are the same width. The verdict was not a refusal, it was a message for the wrong party. `setupR` already took its ciphertext first for this reason; this is the same rule on the sender side.

`pki.merkle.root` and the proof verbs check a hash's width before copying it, and `pki.tuf.verifySignatures` bounds `metadata.signedBytes` before copying it. Both copied first and then refused, so a value handed where a 32-byte hash belongs was duplicated in full: measured, one 64 MiB leaf allocated another 64 MiB, and a 32 MiB `signedBytes` allocated 32 MiB before the comparison rejected it. The signed bytes must equal the canonical form of a body that came from a document no larger than the one-megabyte cap, so anything above that cap cannot match and is refused with `tuf/too-large` rather than copied. A wrong-width hash is refused as before, with the same code.

The `pki` command writes to an existing output destination write-only, so a FIFO reaches a reader rather than the command itself. Opening it for reading as well made the process its own reader: the open succeeded with nobody listening, the bytes went into a pipe no one drains, and `pki csr --out <fifo>` reported success with the output gone, while a larger result blocked. A write-only open waits for a reader, which is what naming a FIFO asks for. The destination is still opened without permission to create it, so a path that stops existing between the two attempts is retried as the exclusive create it has become.

Every report the command line writes keeps to one line, and the escape it uses is unambiguous. A path is given on the command line and fifteen refusals name one, but only the exit handler's reports escaped a carriage return or newline, so a path carrying one printed it raw and whatever followed landed where an operator reads this tool's own output: `pki keygen --pub` over an existing file whose name holds a newline reported across two lines. The escape is now written with two hex digits as well. One digit ran straight into the next character of the path, so a newline followed by `a` printed as `\xaa`, which reads as an escape standing for one byte while it stands for two.

`pki.tls.compressCertificate` and `pki.tuf.checkExpiry` read their size limit before the copy it governs. Both copy their input early on purpose, so that reading a caller option or comparing a body cannot substitute what the verb acts on, and the limit sat after that copy: a 64 MiB certificate message allocated another 64 MiB before the handshake framing limit refused it, and a 64 MiB `metadata.signedBytes` allocated 64 MiB before the canonical-form comparison rejected it. Viewing a value allocates nothing, so the limit is read on the view and only a value within it is copied, which keeps the early copy that closes the substitution window. An option getter still cannot change which message is compressed.

`pki.tls.decompressCertificate` copies the compressed message before it reads its options, so an option getter cannot change which message is decompressed. It held a view of the caller's buffer while resolving `opts.maxOutputBytes`, and reading an option is caller code when it is an accessor: a getter that wrote another well-framed message of the same length over the buffer had the verb decompress the replacement, having framed the one it was handed. `compressCertificate` already took its copy before reading `opts.algorithm`; this is the other half of that pair. The report of a completed write escapes a carriage return or newline in a path as the refusals do, so the success line a script parses stays one line too.

Eight promises the toolkit awaits were built through the live global instead of the constructor captured when the package loaded. `Promise.resolve` builds through its receiver, so handing it `globalThis.Promise` put a correctly captured operation straight back under a constructor a replacement installed afterwards could take over, and what that constructor settles with is the value the toolkit then reads. In `pki.possession.verifyRequest` that value is a certification-path result: a constructor settling with `{ valid: true }` made a correctly signed request report a validated path where there was none, and the RFC 9883 section 4 requirement that the signature certificate's path validate was reported as satisfied without being applied. The same shape sat on the alternative-signature paths of `pki.x509.sign` and `pki.crl.sign` and on three `pki.acme` renewal paths, eight places in all, each now passing the captured constructor.

`pki.scep.parse` read an RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 pkcsPKIEnvelope whatever the outer signature was. That combination over a content with no integrity tag, such as the AES-CBC a deployed SCEP peer sends, is refused by `pki.cms.decrypt` because a rejected key unwrap and a conforming one report different outcomes, and an attacker submitting chosen ciphertexts learns from the difference which theirs was. Reading it anyway rests on the envelope having arrived inside a signature an authorized peer made, and without `opts.signerCert` the signature is any signer's, which this verb states by reporting `signerAuthenticated: false`. An unauthenticated message's envelope is now refused as `scep/decrypt-failed` over `cms/unauthenticated-rsa-v15`. Pass `opts.signerCert` with the peer's certificate to read those messages; it is the same option that binds the transaction attributes to an authorized signer.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` could refuse a bundle that carried a valid certification path, because it searched for that path itself. The local search assembled at most eight paths and ranked candidates by name, so where a CA had rotated and more than eight certificates sharing one subject DN were issued directly by the trusted anchor, those eight were spent on whichever ones the bundle happened to list first and the certificate that actually signed the leaf was never validated: the result was `sigstore/chain-invalid` for a bundle holding a valid path. The search is `pki.path.build` now, which owns it. Candidates are ranked by the RFC 4158 section 3.5 heuristics and none is excluded, and the bound counts candidate expansions against a ceiling of 1000 rather than capping assembled paths at eight, so the same-subject siblings a rotation produces no longer exhaust it. A search that does reach its bound, or a bundle naming more certificates than the search will consider, reports `sigstore/chain-incomplete` rather than a verdict that the chain is invalid. Every assembled path still flows through `pki.path.validate`, so no check is duplicated or relaxed. A bounded depth-first search still spends its budget on the branches it is steered to, so a bundle large enough to exhaust the ceiling can still depend on the order it lists its certificates in; what changed is the size at which that begins.

`pki.tuf.parseMetadata` and `pki.tuf.checkExpiry` accepted an `expires` carrying any time-zone offset, such as `2030-01-01T01:00:00+01:00`. The shared RFC 3339 scanner admits every numeric offset because RFC 3339 does, while the TUF specification section 4.2.3 states the form `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` and that time is always in UTC. Such a value names a real instant but not the one the specification asks for, so a conforming client refuses the document where this adopted it. Both verbs require `Z` or a zero numeric offset now, which denote the same instant; the rule reaches `checkExpiry` as well, because that verb is reachable with a metadata object a caller assembled rather than one `parseMetadata` returned.

`pki.path.build` coerced its candidate pool and forwarded its validation options through the live `Array.prototype.map` and `Object.keys`, so a replacement installed after the package loaded could make a build raise `path/bad-input` and deny a path the pool could assemble. Both take the operation captured at load now.

`pki issue --copy-requested-san` refused every request whose subjectAltName was critical, and that is the one form a SAN-only request must take: RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.6 requires the extension critical where the subject is empty, and `pki lint` refuses the non-critical form as `lint/rfc2986/san-not-critical-empty-subject`. The only conforming empty-subject request was therefore the one this verb would not certify. Copying it loses nothing either, because the certificate builder takes the extension's criticality from the subject it encodes, so an empty subject writes the critical form. The refusal now applies where it is true, to a request that carries a subject, where writing the non-critical form would answer a different request than the one made.

The package could not be required at all with Node FIPS mode enabled. `guard.crypto` captures the three KeyObject `export` methods when it loads, which it does by making one sample key pair to read their prototypes from, and the sample was Ed25519. OpenSSL's FIPS provider carries no Ed25519, so `crypto.setFips(1)` followed by requiring the package raised `ERR_OSSL_EVP_UNSUPPORTED` out of module initialization, and a deployment needing only approved RSA or EC operations could not load the package to reach them. The sample is a P-256 pair now, which is inside the FIPS 140-3 boundary, and one pair yields both prototypes where two were generated before. The prototypes do not depend on the algorithm, so nothing about what is captured changes.

`pki.acme.validate` read every own member of the resource it was handed, including names no ACME specification lists. This surface ignores extension members, and ignoring one means not reading it: an accessor on an unknown name is caller code, so a throwing one left `validate` by a path carrying no `acme/` code, and a side-effecting one ran before the listed fields had been captured, which let it change one the reading had not reached yet, such as the `status` the closed-enum check decides from. Only the fields a resource's specification names are read now, each once. The same applies to the prior window `pki.acme.renewalWindow` compares against.

`pki.cmp.openKeyPackage` opened an RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 delivered key package over a content with no integrity tag without being asked to. The verb takes the container rather than the CMP message that carried it, so it cannot establish that the container arrived inside an authenticated exchange, and the same chosen-ciphertext distinction applies. The decision is now the caller's: pass `allowUnauthenticatedRsa15: true` where the containers this entity opens come from an authenticated exchange. A container using RSAES-OAEP, which this toolkit emits, needs nothing; the password technique never reached the refusal, because it is not key transport.
